items.stem: Which of the following best describes "right to privacy"?
options: An intentional disruption of internet or electronic communications, making them inaccessible or unusable for a population or location
A multi-stakeholder organisation (founded 2008) of companies, NGOs and academics committed to freedom of expression and privacy in the tech sector
The human-rights principle that restrictions on rights must be necessary, the least intrusive option and balanced against their aim
The right to be free from arbitrary interference with one's privacy, family, home and correspondence (UDHR Article 12; ICCPR Article 17)
items.answer: The right to be free from arbitrary interference with one's privacy, family, home and correspondence (UDHR Article 12; ICCPR Article 17)
items.markingKey: D. "right to privacy" is the right to be free from arbitrary interference with one's privacy, family, home and correspondence (UDHR Article 12; ICCPR Article 17).

items.stem: Briefly explain why privacy is described as an enabling right.
items.answer: Privacy allows people to think, communicate, associate and express themselves without fear of surveillance, so it supports other rights such as free expression, assembly and freedom of belief.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Privacy allows people to think, communicate, associate and express themselves without fear of surveillance, so it supports other rights such as free expression, assembly and freedom of belief. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Human-rights law only applies to governments, so platforms have no human-rights responsibilities." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011) say companies have a responsibility to respect human rights, and laws like the DSA require platforms to consider fundamental rights.
items.markingKey: The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011) say companies have a responsibility to respect human rights, and laws like the DSA require platforms to consider fundamental rights. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"No one shall be subjected to arbitrary or unlawful interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence."
— International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 17 (1966)

Explain how this source applies to mass digital surveillance.
items.answer: Bulk interception of communications without individual suspicion may be "arbitrary interference" with correspondence, unless lawful, necessary and proportionate.
items.markingKey: Bulk interception of communications without individual suspicion may be "arbitrary interference" with correspondence, unless lawful, necessary and proportionate. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A transparency report from a social network shows it received 18,000 government requests for user data in six months and produced some data in 85% of cases. On average each request concerned 2 accounts. Calculate the number of requests where data was produced and the number of accounts affected. Explain why transparency reports matter for digital rights.
items.answer: 15,300 requests; about 30,600 accounts; they reveal the scale of state access to personal data, allowing public scrutiny and accountability, though they cannot show secret requests (e.g. gag orders)
items.markingKey: 18,000 × 85% = 15,300 [M1 A1]; × 2 = 30,600 accounts [A1]. Accountability/scrutiny of state surveillance; limitation (secret orders, aggregated data) [R1 R1].

items.stem: Briefly describe Google Spain (2014) and explain what it reveals about the right to be forgotten.
items.answer: Mario Costeja González asked Google to delist old newspaper notices about his debts; the EU Court of Justice ruled search engines must remove links to inadequate, irrelevant or outdated personal data on request, unless public interest outweighs privacy. The case balanced privacy against access to information, and Google has since processed over a million delisting requests.
items.markingKey: Context (Mario Costeja González asked Google to delist old newspaper notices about his debts; the EU Court of Justice ruled search engines must remove links to inadequate, irrelevant or outdated personal data on request, unless public interest outweighs privacy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the case balanced privacy against access to information, and Google has since processed over a million delisting requests. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the right to be forgotten.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Internet access should be recognised as a human right."
items.answer: Recognising access as a right, or as essential to other rights, is justified given how much of life is online, though implementation must be progressive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: access is necessary for exercising many other rights; UN resolutions and some states (e.g. Finland broadband right 2010) recognise it. Arguments against: rights should protect fundamental values, not technologies; costly obligation for poor states; access alone does not guarantee rights (censorship). Supported judgement: Recognising access as a right, or as essential to other rights, is justified given how much of life is online, though implementation must be progressive.

items.stem: Explain why digital rights can conflict with each other.
items.answer: Freedom of expression can conflict with privacy (publishing personal information), with protection from harm (hate speech) or with the right to be forgotten (public-interest information), requiring balancing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Freedom of expression can conflict with privacy (publishing personal information), with protection from harm (hate speech) or with the right to be forgotten (public-interest information), requiring balancing. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why access to the internet is increasingly seen as a human right.
items.answer: So many rights – education, work, expression, information, political participation – are exercised online that lack of access excludes people from enjoying them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: So many rights – education, work, expression, information, political participation – are exercised online that lack of access excludes people from enjoying them. items.stem: Distinguish between a negative right and a positive right.
items.answer: A negative right requires others (especially states) not to interfere (e.g. no censorship); a positive right requires action to provide something (e.g. state measures to ensure internet access).
items.markingKey: A negative right requires others (especially states) not to interfere (e.g. no censorship); a positive right requires action to provide something (e.g. state measures to ensure internet access). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The same rights that people have offline must also be protected online, in particular freedom of expression."
— UN Human Rights Council Resolution 20/8, 2012

With reference to the source, explain its significance for governments.
items.answer: It confirms that existing human-rights obligations apply online, so states cannot censor, surveil or block online expression in ways that would be unlawful offline.
items.markingKey: It confirms that existing human-rights obligations apply online, so states cannot censor, surveil or block online expression in ways that would be unlawful offline. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "mercenary spyware".
items.answer: Commercial surveillance software such as Pegasus or Predator sold to governments to hack phones

items.stem: Explain why censorship is harder to detect online than offline.
items.answer: Throttling, algorithmic down-ranking, selective blocking and deletion can look like technical problems, and users may not know what they cannot see.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Throttling, algorithmic down-ranking, selective blocking and deletion can look like technical problems, and users may not know what they cannot see. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between platform blocking and a full shutdown.
items.answer: A full shutdown cuts all internet access in an area; platform blocking restricts specific services (e.g. X, WhatsApp) while leaving other access.
items.markingKey: A full shutdown cuts all internet access in an area; platform blocking restricts specific services (e.g. X, WhatsApp) while leaving other access. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A government cuts mobile internet in a region of 2 million people for 720 hours during protests. Internet penetration in the region is 45%. Calculate the number of internet users affected and the total "user-hours" of lost access.
items.answer: 0.9 million users; 648 million user-hours
items.markingKey: 2 m × 45% = 0.9 m users [M1 A1]; × 720 h = 648 million user-hours [A1].

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Shutdowns are a blunt instrument: they cut off everyone – the doctor, the journalist, the student – to stop a few."
— UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of expression, report to the Human Rights Council, 2022

With reference to the source, explain why shutdowns fail the proportionality test.
items.answer: They affect the entire population rather than targeting specific wrongdoing, so the harm to rights is excessive compared with their aim.
items.markingKey: They affect the entire population rather than targeting specific wrongdoing, so the harm to rights is excessive compared with their aim. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Evaluate the impacts of one internet shutdown or censorship measure on human rights and on different stakeholders.
items.answer: E.g. Kashmir 2019–21, Manipur 2023, Iran 2019/2022, Russia 2022; rights affected; stakeholders (citizens, journalists, businesses, government); proportionality; responses (courts, VPNs, #KeepItOn); judgement.
items.markingKey: E.g. Kashmir 2019–21, Manipur 2023, Iran 2019/2022, Russia 2022; rights affected; stakeholders (citizens, journalists, businesses, government); proportionality; responses (courts, VPNs, #KeepItOn); judgement.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "censorship"?
options: The right to have certain personal information removed from search results, established by the EU Court of Justice in Google Spain (2014)
The suppression or prohibition of information or expression considered objectionable or threatening by authorities
A multi-stakeholder organisation (founded 2008) of companies, NGOs and academics committed to freedom of expression and privacy in the tech sector
The human-rights principle that restrictions on rights must be necessary, the least intrusive option and balanced against their aim
items.answer: The suppression or prohibition of information or expression considered objectionable or threatening by authorities
items.markingKey: B. "censorship" is the suppression or prohibition of information or expression considered objectionable or threatening by authorities.

items.stem: "Using a VPN always defeats censorship." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: VPNs can be blocked, detected by deep packet inspection, banned by law or unusable during full shutdowns.
items.markingKey: VPNs can be blocked, detected by deep packet inspection, banned by law or unusable during full shutdowns. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Russia's throttling of Twitter (2021) and blocking after 2022 shows state censorship.
items.answer: Russia slowed Twitter in 2021 and blocked Facebook, Instagram and Twitter after its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while VPN use surged. The state used technical controls to restrict independent information, while citizens resisted with VPNs.
items.markingKey: Context (Russia slowed Twitter in 2021 and blocked Facebook, Instagram and Twitter after its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while VPN use surged.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the state used technical controls to restrict independent information, while citizens resisted with VPNs. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to state censorship.

items.stem: Using the Pegasus Project (2021) as an example, explain surveillance as a human-rights challenge.
items.answer: A leak of 50,000 phone numbers of potential targets and forensic analysis by Amnesty International linked NSO's Pegasus to surveillance of journalists and activists, including people close to Jamal Khashoggi. Commercial spyware gave states powerful tools to target civil society, prompting US sanctions and EU inquiries.
items.markingKey: Context (A leak of 50,000 phone numbers of potential targets and forensic analysis by Amnesty International linked NSO's Pegasus to surveillance of journalists and activists, including people close to Jamal Khashoggi.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: A global moratorium until strong safeguards exist is justified, with strict export controls and accountability.

items.answer: strategic litigation

items.stem: Explain the difference between strategic litigation and advocacy campaigns.
items.answer: Strategic litigation uses courts to create binding legal change (e.g. Schrems cases); advocacy campaigns use public pressure, research and lobbying (e.g. #KeepItOn) to influence governments and companies.
items.markingKey: Strategic litigation uses courts to create binding legal change (e.g. Schrems cases); advocacy campaigns use public pressure, research and lobbying (e.g. #KeepItOn) to influence governments and companies. items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why international law is often weak in protecting digital rights.
items.answer: Enforcement depends on states' willingness, many key actors are private companies, technology outpaces treaties and powerful states may refuse to sign or comply. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Enforcement depends on states' willingness, many key actors are private companies, technology outpaces treaties and powerful states may refuse to sign or comply. items.stem: Aiko writes: "Only governments can protect digital rights." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Courts, civil-society organisations, journalists, standards bodies and companies (through encryption, transparency reports) also play key roles.
items.markingKey: Courts, civil-society organisations, journalists, standards bodies and companies (through encryption, transparency reports) also play key roles. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the #KeepItOn coalition and explain what it reveals about civil-society interventions.
items.answer: Access Now's #KeepItOn coalition of hundreds of organisations tracks shutdowns, publishes annual reports and lobbies governments and telecom companies. Documentation and advocacy raise the cost of shutdowns, though many governments continue to impose them.
items.markingKey: Context (Access Now's #KeepItOn coalition of hundreds of organisations tracks shutdowns, publishes annual reports and lobbies governments and telecom companies.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Evaluate one intervention by an international organisation, government or civil-society group designed to protect digital rights.
items.answer: E.g. Council of Europe AI Convention, #KeepItOn, Marco Civil, US sanctions on NSO, GDPR; aims, stakeholders, effectiveness, limitations, recommendation.

items.stem: Which civil-society campaign, coordinated by Access Now, campaigns against internet shutdowns?

items.stem: Distinguish between international law and national law.
items.answer: International law (treaties, UN resolutions) sets standards across states but has weak enforcement; national law (e.g. Brazil's Marco Civil, India's DPDP Act) is directly enforceable but limited to one country.

Read the source below.

"We built the Marco Civil with the people, through the internet itself."
— Brazilian official describing the online consultation for the Marco Civil, 2014

items.answer: Public participation gave the law democratic legitimacy and incorporated many perspectives, making it more likely to reflect citizens' rights and needs.

items.stem: Using Brazil's Marco Civil da Internet (2014) as an example, explain digital constitutionalism.
items.answer: Developed through online public consultation, the law sets principles of net neutrality, privacy and freedom of expression and limits intermediary liability. A participatory process produced a rights-based framework for the internet at national level.
items.markingKey: Context (Developed through online public consultation, the law sets principles of net neutrality, privacy and freedom of expression and limits intermediary liability.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Distinguish between privacy and data protection.
items.answer: Privacy is a broad right to a private life free from interference; data protection is a specific set of rules governing how personal data is processed (e.g. GDPR), recognised separately in the EU Charter.

items.stem: Distinguish between content moderation and censorship.
items.answer: Censorship is suppression of expression by authorities, often political; content moderation is a platform enforcing its rules or the law on its service – though states can pressure platforms to censor.

items.stem: Briefly explain why civil society plays an important role in protecting digital rights.
items.answer: NGOs and journalists investigate abuses (Pegasus Project), document shutdowns, bring strategic litigation and advocate for laws, holding states and companies accountable when they are unwilling to regulate themselves.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017) shows privacy as a constitutional right.
items.answer: India's Supreme Court unanimously recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution. The ruling became the basis for limiting Aadhaar and for the DPDP Act 2023.

"Business enterprises should respect human rights. This means that they should avoid infringing on the human rights of others and should address adverse human rights impacts with which they are involved."

items.stem: Define the term "proportionality".
items.answer: The human-rights principle that restrictions on rights must be necessary, the least intrusive option and balanced against their aim

items.stem: In 2023, how long was Manipur in India under an internet shutdown after ethnic violence began?
items.answer: About seven months (May to December)
items.markingKey: C. Mobile internet was largely suspended from May 2023.

items.stem: Define the term "Global Network Initiative".
items.answer: A multi-stakeholder organisation (founded 2008) of companies, NGOs and academics committed to freedom of expression and privacy in the tech sector

items.stem: A student claims: "Freedom of expression means all speech must be allowed online." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Human-rights law permits restrictions that are lawful, necessary and proportionate, e.g. incitement to violence or child sexual abuse material.
items.markingKey: Human-rights law permits restrictions that are lawful, necessary and proportionate, e.g. incitement to violence or child sexual abuse material. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Internet shutdowns only happen in authoritarian states." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Democracies also impose shutdowns – India records many regional shutdowns – often citing public order or exams.
items.markingKey: Democracies also impose shutdowns – India records many regional shutdowns – often citing public order or exams. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between international law and national law.
items.answer: International law (treaties, UN resolutions) sets standards across states but has weak enforcement; national law (e.g. Brazil's Marco Civil, India's DPDP Act) is directly enforceable but limited to one country.
items.markingKey: International law (treaties, UN resolutions) sets standards across states but has weak enforcement; national law (e.g. Brazil's Marco Civil, India's DPDP Act) is directly enforceable but limited to one country. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Human-rights law only applies to governments, so platforms have no human-rights responsibilities." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011) say companies have a responsibility to respect human rights, and laws like the DSA require platforms to consider fundamental rights.
items.markingKey: The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011) say companies have a responsibility to respect human rights, and laws like the DSA require platforms to consider fundamental rights. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between censorship and content moderation.
items.answer: Censorship is suppression of expression by authorities, often political; content moderation is a platform enforcing its rules or the law on its service – though states can pressure platforms to censor.
items.markingKey: Censorship is suppression of expression by authorities, often political; content moderation is a platform enforcing its rules or the law on its service – though states can pressure platforms to censor. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why digital constitutionalism has emerged.
items.answer: Platforms and digital states exercise power over rights in ways traditional constitutions did not foresee, so courts, legislators and civil society seek to limit this power through rights charters and laws such as the DSA or Marco Civil.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Platforms and digital states exercise power over rights in ways traditional constitutions did not foresee, so courts, legislators and civil society seek to limit this power through rights charters and laws such as the DSA or Marco Civil. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which Google Spain (2014) shows the right to be forgotten.
items.answer: Mario Costeja González asked Google to delist old newspaper notices about his debts; the EU Court of Justice ruled search engines must remove links to inadequate, irrelevant or outdated personal data on request, unless public interest outweighs privacy. The case balanced privacy against access to information, and Google has since processed over a million delisting requests.
items.markingKey: Context (Mario Costeja González asked Google to delist old newspaper notices about his debts; the EU Court of Justice ruled search engines must remove links to inadequate, irrelevant or outdated personal data on request, unless public interest outweighs privacy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: A government cuts mobile internet in a region of 2 million people for 72 hours during protests. Internet penetration in the region is 75%. Calculate the number of internet users affected and the total "user-hours" of lost access.
items.answer: 1.5 million users; 108 million user-hours
items.markingKey: 2 m × 75% = 1.5 m users [M1 A1]; × 72 h = 108 million user-hours [A1].

items.stem: Using Max Schrems and noyb as an example, explain strategic litigation by civil society.
items.answer: Austrian lawyer Max Schrems brought complaints that led the EU Court of Justice to invalidate Safe Harbour (2015) and Privacy Shield (2020); his NGO noyb has filed hundreds of GDPR complaints. One activist used courts to force changes to transatlantic data flows, showing the power of rights-based litigation.

items.stem: Using Schrems II (2020) as an example, explain privacy across borders.
items.answer: Austrian activist Max Schrems challenged transfers of his Facebook data to the US; the EU Court of Justice invalidated the Privacy Shield because of US surveillance laws. An individual's complaint reshaped global data flows, showing how rights litigation can constrain both states and companies.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Internet shutdowns can be justified during periods of violent unrest."
items.answer: Shutdowns are almost never justified; targeted, lawful measures against specific illegal content are more proportionate.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: governments claim they stop rumours and coordination of violence; short, local measures in emergencies. Arguments against: evidence suggests shutdowns do not reduce violence and may increase it; block emergency services and reporting of abuses (Manipur); violate proportionality. Supported judgement: Shutdowns are almost never justified; targeted, lawful measures against specific illegal content are more proportionate.

items.stem: "Civil society is more effective than international law in protecting digital rights." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Civil society and international law are complementary: NGOs use legal standards to hold actors accountable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: investigations (Pegasus Project) and litigation (Schrems) produce concrete change; fast and flexible. Arguments against: NGOs lack enforcement power; governments may restrict civil society; international standards give NGOs a basis for advocacy. Supported judgement: Civil society and international law are complementary: NGOs use legal standards to hold actors accountable. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Internet access should be recognised as a human right."
items.answer: Recognising access as a right, or as essential to other rights, is justified given how much of life is online, though implementation must be progressive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: access is necessary for exercising many other rights; UN resolutions and some states (e.g. Finland broadband right 2010) recognise it. Arguments against: rights should protect fundamental values, not technologies; costly obligation for poor states; access alone does not guarantee rights (censorship).
